SAP BTP Foundations · Task 01 · Zero → Hero

From never having touched SAP, to a live deploy on it.

This is a complete walkthrough — concepts, setup, and the hands-on task. By the end, you will have provisioned SAP BTP, built a real service, and deployed it to a public URL. No prior SAP, cloud, or programming experience required. Bring focus, stay with it, and you'll be done sooner than you think.

Part One

Understand the platform first.

Before any commands, the concepts. Skim or read in depth — by the end of this section, every piece of SAP terminology in the task will already make sense.

Concept 01

What is SAP BTP?

SAP BTP stands for Business Technology Platform. It's SAP's cloud platform — think of it like AWS or Azure, but built specifically for extending and building around SAP business systems (like S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, Ariba).

If you've used AWS, the mental model is similar: you get an account, you provision services inside it (databases, compute runtimes, identity providers), and you build apps that use those services.

In one sentence

SAP BTP is where you build, host, secure, and integrate cloud apps in the SAP ecosystem.

What you can do on it

  • Build custom applications — like the one you'll build today, using SAP's frameworks
  • Run databases — SAP HANA Cloud is the flagship; PostgreSQL is also available
  • Wire integrations — connect to SAP S/4HANA, Salesforce, or any external system
  • Add AI / automation — chatbots, document processing, process automation
  • Manage identity — OAuth, SAML, role-based access

For Task 1, you'll only touch a small slice of this: provisioning a free trial, using the development tools, and deploying one small service. But everything you learn applies to the rest.

Concept 02

The account hierarchy.

SAP BTP organizes everything into a four-level hierarchy. Understanding this saves you from a lot of confusion later. The four levels, from outermost to innermost:

Each level wraps the one inside it. Your apps live at the innermost level.

What each level is for, in plain English

  1. Global Account — the whole pie. One per organization (or one per trial user, in your case). Holds your entitlements, your billing, your top-level admin.
  2. Subaccount — a workspace within the global account. Most companies have several (one for dev, one for QA, one for prod). Trial users get exactly one, called trial.
  3. Cloud Foundry Org — a runtime boundary. You don't really interact with the org level often; it just exists because Cloud Foundry (the runtime SAP uses) requires it.
  4. Space — where your deployed apps actually live. Like a folder for your running code. You'll deploy your app into a space called dev.
Concept 03

The cockpit.

The cockpit is SAP BTP's web interface. Everything you can do via CLI, you can also do here. It's where you'll spend the first part of the task.

The actual cockpit: top bar with your avatar, left sidebar for navigation, breadcrumb at the top, and your subaccount tile in the main area.

The three things you actually need to know about the cockpit

  1. The left sidebar is how you navigate between sections of an account (Subaccounts, Entitlements, Security, etc.).
  2. The breadcrumb at the top tells you where you are in the hierarchy. Click any part of it to jump back up.
  3. The tile in the main area is your subaccount — click into it to see its services and spaces.
Concept 04

What is Cloud Foundry?

Cloud Foundry (CF) is a runtime — the thing that actually runs your code after you deploy it. SAP didn't invent it; CF is an open-source platform that SAP uses inside BTP.

The mental model: if your code is a passenger, CF is the airplane. CF takes care of everything around the actual running of your code — networking, scaling, logging, restarts, routing requests to the right instance.

In one sentence

Cloud Foundry is the runtime that hosts your deployed apps. You build code; CF runs it and gives it a URL.

What CF does for you

  • Takes your built code (an MTA archive) and runs it
  • Assigns it a public HTTPS URL (the "route")
  • Provides services like databases that your app can use
  • Restarts your app if it crashes
  • Streams logs you can read to debug problems
Concept 05

What is CAP?

CAP stands for Cloud Application Programming Model. It's SAP's framework for building services — kind of like Spring Boot for Java or Express for Node, but with one huge superpower: it generates a working OData service from a tiny data model.

CAP turns a short data model into a complete CRUD API. No controllers to write.

In Task 1, you won't even write the data model yourself — you'll use a built-in sample (a bookshop). That way, you can focus on the platform mechanics first, and learn the modeling later.

Concept 06

What is OData?

OData is a standard for building REST APIs — basically a set of rules about how URLs, query parameters, and JSON responses should look. SAP uses OData everywhere because it's predictable, well-documented, and tooling-friendly.

You'll see URLs that look like this in your work today:

https://<your-app>.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com/odata/v4/catalog/Books

Breaking it down:

  • /odata/v4 — "this is an OData v4 endpoint"
  • /catalog — the service name (you can have many services per app)
  • /Books — the entity (like a database table you're querying)

The response is plain JSON. Browsers can hit it directly. Tools like Postman work fine. Front-end frameworks can consume it without ceremony.

Concept 07

What is Business Application Studio?

Business Application Studio (BAS) is a cloud-based code editor — Visual Studio Code, but in your browser, pre-configured for SAP development. It's where you'll do all the actual building work in Task 1.

Why use BAS instead of VS Code on your laptop?

Because BAS comes pre-installed with every SAP tool you need: cds (CAP CLI), mbt (the build tool), cf, node, git. No setup on your machine. And it runs inside SAP BTP, which makes some things (like authentication) easier.

You'll create something called a Dev Space inside BAS. That's like a tiny pre-configured Linux machine in the cloud, dedicated to your project.

Concept 08

The two command-line tools.

SAP gives you two CLI tools, and you'll use both. They work at different levels of the hierarchy.

Two CLIs, two scopes. They share authentication context but address different layers.

Memorable shorthand: btp = the platform stuff. cf = the running-code stuff. If your command is about managing the account, you want btp. If your command is about your deployed app, you want cf.

Concept 09

Put it all together.

Here's the full flow of what you're about to do, with everything you've just learned:

Your authenticated CLIs let you talk to BTP. BAS is where you code. CF runs your app. Your browser hits the live URL.
Knowledge check

Make sure these clicked before moving on. (Click to reveal each answer.)

1. What's the difference between a Global Account and a Subaccount?
Show the answer
A Global Account is the whole container — like an entire company's BTP presence. A Subaccount is a workspace inside it (e.g., one for dev, one for prod). Trial users get one of each: the global account is your overall trial; the single subaccount inside is called "trial".
2. Which command-line tool would you use to deploy a built application?
Show the answer
cf. The btp CLI is for managing accounts and subaccounts. The cf CLI is for everything that happens to your running app — deploying, viewing logs, restarting, scaling.
3. Why is CAP useful?
Show the answer
CAP takes a tiny data model (like "Books has a title and an author") and automatically generates a full CRUD OData service from it. You skip writing controllers, validation, and most boilerplate.
4. What is BAS used for?
Show the answer
It's a cloud-based code editor (like VS Code in the browser) that comes pre-installed with every SAP development tool. You'll use it to write code, run a local dev server, and build deployable artifacts.
Good stopping point

End of Part 1. If you can answer "what's BTP?", "what's CAP?", and "what's Cloud Foundry?" in your own words — even roughly — you've got the conceptual base. Part 2 is hands-on setup (no thinking, just installing). Come back to it fresh, ideally still on the same day so the concepts stay warm.

Part Two

Set up your tools.

Four things to install or sign up for. Do all of them — the task itself assumes everything here works.

S1Setup

Create an SAP BTP Trial account.

⏱ 10 min🌐 In your browser

Free, no credit card. Takes 5-10 minutes.

Step by step

  1. Open sap.com/products/technology-platform/trial.html.
  2. Click Try Now.
  3. Use a personal email (Gmail, Outlook, etc.) — not your work email. Corporate domains often get rejected.
  4. Register an SAP Universal ID if you don't have one. Check your email and click the verification link.
  5. Set a password and accept the terms.
  6. Verify your phone via SMS code.
  7. Company / Department fields: these aren't validated. Use Personal and Learning if you have nothing else.
  8. On the welcome page, click Go To Your Trial Account.
  9. Bookmark the page you land on — that's your cockpit URL.
90 days, but with a catch

Your trial lasts 90 days total, but SAP auto-deletes accounts that go 30 consecutive days without a login. Set a calendar reminder to log in once a week to keep it alive.

S2Setup

Install Node.js (LTS version).

⏱ 5 min💻 On your laptop

Node.js is the runtime CAP uses on your laptop while you develop. You need version 20 or higher.

Install

  1. Go to nodejs.org.
  2. Download the LTS version for your operating system.
  3. Run the installer with default options. Click through.
On nodejs.org, click the green Get Node.js® button. (LTS is selected by default — that's what you want.)
On the download page, scroll down and click Windows Installer (.msi) for the prebuilt download. Run it with all defaults.

Verify

If you've never opened a terminal before

A terminal (also called a "command line" or "shell") is just a text-based way to give your computer instructions. Instead of clicking buttons, you type a command and press Enter. The window that opens is usually black or dark with one line of text waiting for you — that's normal, not an error. You cannot break your computer by typing in it. Every developer uses one daily; this is the moment you start.

Open a fresh terminal:

  • Windows: press the Windows key, type "PowerShell", hit Enter.
  • Mac: press ⌘+Space, type "Terminal", hit Enter.
  • Linux: you know how to open a terminal.

Then type this command and press Enter:

node --version

You should see something like v20.18.0 or higher. If you see "command not found", don't worry — this happens to everyone the first time. The fix: close your terminal window completely and open a fresh one. The new one will pick up the Node install.

S3Setup

Install Git.

⏱ 5 min💻 On your laptop

Git is the version-control system. You won't use it directly in Task 1, but BAS expects it to be available.

Install

  1. Go to git-scm.com.
  2. Download the installer for your OS.
  3. Run with defaults. (On Windows, the installer asks a lot of questions — click Next on all of them.)
On git-scm.com, the right-side panel auto-detects your OS. Click Install for Windows (or your platform's equivalent).

Verify

git --version

You should see something like git version 2.43.0.

S4Setup

Set up GitHub.

⏱ 10 min🌐 In your browser

You probably won't push code to GitHub during Task 1, but you'll create an account and generate an access token — it's useful for future tasks, and getting it now means you don't break flow later.

Sign up

  1. Go to github.com.
  2. Click Sign up. Use any email; pick a username and password.
  3. Verify your email.

Create a personal access token

  1. Click your profile picture (top-right) → Settings.
  2. Scroll the left sidebar all the way to the bottom → Developer settings.
  3. Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic) → Generate new token (classic).
  4. Note: sap-btp-course. Expiration: 90 days. Scope: tick the repo checkbox.
  5. Click Generate token.
  6. Copy the token immediately — paste it into a notes app. GitHub only shows it once.
Step 1. Click your profile picture (top-right) and pick Settings from the dropdown.
Step 2. Scroll the left sidebar all the way down. The very last item is Developer settings.
Step 3. Pick Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic), then click Generate new token. (Use the classic variant — fine-grained tokens add complexity you don't need here.)
Don't lose the token

If you lose the token, you can't recover it — you'd have to delete it and generate a new one. Save it somewhere persistent.

Verify all four are done.

Quick checklist. If you can tick all four, you're ready to start the task.

Setup checklist
  • ☐ I can log into the SAP BTP cockpit and I see one subaccount called trial
  • ☐ node --version returns v20 or higher
  • ☐ git --version returns a version
  • ☐ I have a GitHub account and a personal access token saved somewhere
You're set

Everything from here on uses these four tools. You've already done the parts most people quit during — congrats.

Good stopping point — strongly recommended

This is the longest natural pause in the doc. Part 3 is the actual task: 3–4 focused hours. If it's late, or you're tired, or you have less than 2 uninterrupted hours, stop here. Bookmark this page, close the tab, and pick up Part 3 when you have a clean block of time. Doing Part 3 tired is the #1 reason people get stuck on Step 6.

Part Three

The task: deploy your first service.

Seven steps. About 3–4 hours of work — split it across two sessions if you want. By the end, you have a live URL on real SAP cloud infrastructure.

First, the one thing that confuses everyone: two terminals.

A "terminal" is just a window where you type commands instead of clicking buttons. In this task you will use two different terminals, and they are not the same window. Knowing which one a step wants is the single biggest source of confusion — so here is the whole story up front. Every step below also carries a coloured badge telling you exactly which one to use.

💻 Terminal A — Laptop terminal

The one already on your computer.

This is the terminal app built into your machine. You open it yourself, outside the browser.

  • Windows: press the Windows key, type PowerShell, press Enter.
  • Mac: press ⌘ + Space, type Terminal, press Enter.

Used in this task for: installing the two CLIs (Step 3) and the parity drills (Step 4).

🌐 Terminal B — BAS terminal

The one inside the SAP website.

BAS (Business Application Studio) is a code editor that runs in your browser. It has its own terminal built in.

  • Open BAS from the SAP cockpit (Step 5 walks you through it).
  • Inside BAS, click the top menu → Terminal → New Terminal.

Used in this task for: building the project (Step 5) and deploying it (Step 6).

They do not share memory

The two terminals are completely separate. If you log in or install something in the Laptop terminal, the BAS terminal will not know about it — and vice versa. That is why Step 6 asks you to log in again even though you already logged in earlier. It is expected, not a mistake.

Before you start: when you get stuck (and you will)

Every single person who has done this hit a wall at least once. The wall might be a cryptic error message, a step that doesn't quite match what's on your screen, or a command that just sits there. That isn't you being bad at this — that's how learning real platforms works for everyone.

When it happens:

  1. Read the actual error message slowly. Half of them tell you the fix in plain English.
  2. Re-read the step. You'll often spot a missed line.
  3. Google the error message verbatim. SAP BTP has a strong community and most errors are well-documented.
  4. Ask a peer or your trainer. Stuck for >20 min on the same issue is a signal to ask, not a sign of weakness.

Also: if a word is unfamiliar at any point, flip to the glossary at the end of this doc — most jargon is defined there in plain English.

01Task

Land in the cockpit.

⏱ 10 min🌐 In your browser

The first task is just to get oriented. You'll be back in this interface many times.

  1. Log into your trial account (the bookmark from setup).
  2. You should see a "Welcome to SAP BTP Trial" page. Click the blue Go To Your Trial Account button.
After signup, this is the landing page. Click Go To Your Trial Account to enter the cockpit. Quick Tool Access tiles (BAS, CLI, APIs) sit lower on the page — you'll come back here often.
  1. You'll land in the Global Account view. The URL changes to something like account.hanatrial.ondemand.com.
  2. Look around the left sidebar. The most important section is Account Explorer — that's where your subaccount tile lives.
  3. You should see exactly one tile in the main area: trial. Provider: AWS. Region: US East (VA).
Inside your global account, Account Explorer is where subaccounts live. Trial gets exactly one: the trial tile on AWS, US East (VA). Click into it to see what's inside.

Write these down — you'll need them later

Capture from the cockpit
Global account subdomain
At the top of the Global Account view. Looks like <random>trial-ga
Subaccount subdomain
Click into the subaccount to see it. Looks like <random>trial
Trial region
Almost certainly us10
02Task

Confirm Cloud Foundry is ready.

⏱ 5 min🌐 In the cockpit (browser)

Cloud Foundry (the runtime that will host your app) should already be set up on your trial. You're just confirming and capturing a couple of values.

  1. Click the trial subaccount tile.
  2. You land on the subaccount overview. Scroll down to Cloud Foundry Environment.
  3. You should see an API Endpoint, an Org Name, and a Space called dev.
The subaccount overview. The Cloud Foundry Environment panel is the one you'll quote in your terminal: the API Endpoint (notice the -001 suffix), Org Name, and the default dev space.
Capture from the Cloud Foundry section
API Endpoint
https://api.cf.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com
Org Name
The unique string ending in trial
Space
dev
Don't miss the -001

The endpoint has us10-001, not just us10. SAP added the -001 to disambiguate landscapes. Copy it exactly — if you skip it, the cf login will fail later.

If you see "Enable Cloud Foundry" instead

Click it. Plan: standard. Wait ~30 seconds, then create a space called dev and assign yourself the SpaceDeveloper role.

03Task

Install the two CLIs.

⏱ 25 min💻 On your laptop
💻 Use Terminal A — your Laptop terminal (PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on Mac)

Time to install the command-line tools we talked about earlier.

Install the btp CLI

Mac:

brew install --cask btp
btp --version

Windows:

  1. Open tools.hana.ondemand.com.
  2. Press Ctrl+F, search for "SAP BTP Command Line Interface". Don't be fooled by the Neo Java SDKs near the top — those are the wrong (legacy) product.
  3. Download the Windows zip (e.g., btp-cli-windows-amd64-2.x.x.zip).
  4. Unzip into a permanent folder, e.g., C:\btp.
If you double-click btp.exe

A terminal will pop up and close in two seconds. That's not an error. CLIs are meant to be run from inside an existing terminal, not double-clicked.

Open PowerShell. cd into the folder where you unzipped:

cd C:\btp\btp-cli-windows-amd64-2.x.x\windows-amd64
.\btp.exe --version

You should see something like SAP BTP command line interface (client v2.106.1).

Optional: add btp to your Windows PATH

So you can type btp from anywhere instead of .\btp.exe from the install folder. Press Windows key, search "Environment Variables", edit your user-level Path, add the folder. Open a fresh terminal afterwards.

If "environment variables" sound foreign, skip this entirely. Using .\btp.exe everywhere works perfectly fine for everything in this task — you'll never hit a wall because of it.

Install the cf CLI (v8)

  1. Go to github.com/cloudfoundry/cli/releases.
  2. Find the most recent v8.x release.
  3. Windows: download cf8-cli-installer_*_winx64.zip. Unzip. Run the .msi. (The installer auto-adds it to PATH.)
    Mac: brew install cloudfoundry/tap/cf-cli@8
    Linux: follow the apt/yum instructions on the GitHub wiki.
  4. Open a fresh terminal. Verify: cf --version returns v8.x.

Log into both

btp login --url https://cli.btp.cloud.sap
# Email:     your trial email
# Password:  your trial password
# Subdomain: <your-global-account-subdomain>     (the -ga one)
cf login -a https://api.cf.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com
# Email + password
# It'll auto-select org and space (only one of each in trial)
btp login complete. The green Authentication successful line confirms it. Notice the Current target is your global account — the CLI now knows where you live.
cf login complete. A clean run shows OK, then Targeted org = your subaccount and Targeted space = dev. Both CLIs are now authenticated against the same trial.

Verify both work

btp list accounts/subaccount    # lists your trial subaccount
cf target                       # shows your org and dev space
04Task

CLI parity drills.

⏱ 15 min💻 Laptop terminal — Terminal A
💻 Use Terminal A — your Laptop terminal, the same window from Step 3

You just looked at your subaccount in the cockpit. Now do the equivalent from the terminal — both surfaces should feel native.

Run each command and read what comes back. No cockpit allowed.

btp list accounts/subaccount
btp list accounts/entitlement
btp list security/user

cf orgs
cf spaces
cf apps                # empty for now — about to change
cf services            # empty for now
cf marketplace         # ~80 services available in your region
What you should see

cf marketplace returns a long list of available services (HANA Cloud, XSUAA, Destination, etc.). cf apps and cf services should both be empty. btp list accounts/entitlement shows everything your trial is entitled to use.

You're halfway there

By this point you've provisioned a real cloud platform, installed two CLIs, and queried your account from both interfaces. That's already more than most people who say they've "used SAP BTP" can actually do.

05Task

Scaffold a CAP project in BAS.

⏱ 30 min🌐 BAS terminal — Terminal B (in browser)
🌐 Use Terminal B — the BAS terminal, inside the browser (Menu → Terminal → New Terminal)

Now the fun part. You'll open BAS, scaffold a CAP project, and see a working OData service running locally before you ever deploy.

Open BAS

  1. Back in the cockpit, click Trial Home at the top.
  2. Under Quick Tool Access, click SAP Business Application Studio.
  3. If it's not subscribed yet: Create / Subscribe → plan: free. Wait ~1 min.
  4. You also need a role collection or BAS will refuse to load:
    1. Cockpit → trial subaccount → Security → Role Collections
    2. Find Business_Application_Studio_Developer → click → Edit
    3. Under Users, add your trial email → Save
  5. Open BAS via Go to Application.
First time opening BAS, you'll see this privacy statement modal. Tick Do not show this message again if you like, then click OK.

Create a Dev Space

  1. In BAS, click Create Dev Space.
  2. Name: cap_hello (or cap-hello — either is fine).
  3. Type: Full-Stack Application Using Productivity Tools OR Full Stack Cloud Application. Both work.
  4. Click Create Dev Space. Wait ~1–2 min for status Running.
  5. Click the dev space name to open it.
The BAS launchpad showing your dev space. If you come back to BAS after a break, your dev space may be stopped (BAS auto-stops idle ones to save resources) — just click Start Dev Space to bring it back. Nothing is lost.

Verify tools inside BAS

Top menu → Terminal → New Terminal. Run:

node --version    # v20+ or v22+
cds --version     # 9.x or higher
git --version
mbt --version

All four should return versions.

Scaffold the CAP project

mkdir -p ~/projects && cd ~/projects
cds init hello-btp
cd hello-btp
cds add sample
npm install
cds watch

What each does:

  • cds init hello-btp — generates the project skeleton (package.json, srv/, db/, app/)
  • cds add sample — drops in a bookshop sample data model
  • npm install — installs dependencies (don't skip this)
  • cds watch — starts a local dev server with hot reload

When cds watch runs successfully, you'll see:

[cds] - server listening on { url: 'http://localhost:4004' }

BAS pops a notification: "A service is listening on port 4004… Open in a New Tab." Click it.

The CAP welcome page, running locally. cds watch serves it at http://localhost:4004. The interesting bit is Service Endpoints: /odata/v4/admin and /odata/v4/catalog are the two services CAP generated from your data model. Clicking any entity (Books, Authors…) opens a live Fiori preview.

See the data flow

On the welcome page, click /odata/v4/catalog → click Books. You should see JSON with bookshop sample data.

Pause and notice this

You wrote zero code. CAP took the sample data model and generated a complete CRUD OData service automatically. This is the superpower we talked about in Part 1. The same model deployed to production will work the same way.

Stop the dev server: Ctrl+C in the terminal.

06Task

Deploy to real Cloud Foundry.

⏱ 45 min🌐 BAS terminal — Terminal B (in browser)
🌐 Use Terminal B — the BAS terminal again. It does NOT remember Step 3's login, so you log in fresh here

The moment. You'll take what's running locally and ship it to real SAP BTP infrastructure. By the end of this step, anyone with the URL can hit your service.

Why this step has the most commands

"Deploy" sounds like one button, but production CAP is a different runtime from cds watch. You need (a) a deployment descriptor (MTA), (b) a security package CAP requires at boot, and (c) explicit config telling CAP which database and which auth strategy to use — none of which production auto-bootstraps for you. Follow the commands in order.

Make sure you're in the project

cd ~/projects/hello-btp

Generate the MTA descriptor

cds add mta

Creates mta.yaml — the Cloud Foundry deployment manifest. Think of it as the build & deploy instructions for the cloud.

Add the production auth package

npm add @sap/xssec

CAP's production mode boots with JWT authentication wired in. Even though you'll override it in a minute, the @sap/xssec package has to be present or the app won't start at all.

Edit package.json directly

This is the trickiest part of the whole task — and the part most beginners get stuck on. We'll go slow.

If you've never edited a JSON file

JSON is a way to write structured information using { } braces, " " quoted keys, and commas. Three rules will keep you out of trouble:

  1. Curly braces { ... } group related things together.
  2. Items inside a group are separated by commas.
  3. The last item in a group has NO trailing comma.

That's it. If you break a rule, BAS will underline the offending line in red and tell you exactly what's wrong. Stay calm, fix the comma, save again.

Open the file

In BAS, look at the left sidebar — there's a file tree showing your project. Find package.json at the top of the project root. Double-click it. It opens in the editor on the right.

What it looks like right now

After your cds init, npm add @sap/xssec, and cds add mta, your package.json should look something like this:

{
  "name": "hello-btp",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "dependencies": {
    "@sap/cds": "^9",
    "@sap/xssec": "^4"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@cap-js/sqlite": "^2.4",
    "@sap/cds-dk": "^9"
  },
  "scripts": { "start": "cds-serve" },
  "private": true,
  "engines": { "node": ">=20" }
}

Your version numbers may differ slightly. The order of entries inside each block may differ too. That's all fine — JSON doesn't care about order, only structure.

You're going to make two changes.

Change 1 — Move @cap-js/sqlite from devDependencies to dependencies

Why this matters: Cloud Foundry's build step runs with NPM_CONFIG_PRODUCTION=true, which tells npm install to skip every package listed under devDependencies. If @cap-js/sqlite stays in devDependencies, it never gets installed in production. Your app will start fine, but the first time you hit a data endpoint it crashes with 500 NO_DATABASE_CONNECTION — which is exactly what we're preventing.

The mechanic, step by step:

  1. Inside devDependencies, click on the line "@cap-js/sqlite": "^2.4", to place your cursor there. Select the entire line (Home key, then Shift+End on Windows; or triple-click the line).
  2. Cut it: Ctrl+X (Windows) or Cmd+X (Mac).
  3. Scroll up to dependencies. Click at the very end of the "@sap/xssec": "^4" line — your cursor should be right after the closing quote.
  4. Type a comma , and press Enter to start a new line.
  5. Paste: Ctrl+V (Windows) or Cmd+V (Mac).
  6. The pasted line will have a trailing comma at the end. Since this line is now the last entry in dependencies, delete that trailing comma.
  7. Look back at devDependencies. Only "@sap/cds-dk" is left. If there's any stray comma after it (a leftover from when @cap-js/sqlite used to be there), delete that too.

After Change 1, your file should look like this:

{
  "name": "hello-btp",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "dependencies": {
    "@sap/cds": "^9",
    "@sap/xssec": "^4",
    "@cap-js/sqlite": "^2.4"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@sap/cds-dk": "^9"
  },
  "scripts": { "start": "cds-serve" },
  "private": true,
  "engines": { "node": ">=20" }
}
Don't try to "fix" this with npm install --save

You might be tempted to skip the manual edit and just run npm uninstall @cap-js/sqlite followed by npm install --save @cap-js/sqlite. Don't. npm sometimes leaves entries where they are, sometimes silently duplicates them across both blocks. Hand-editing is faster and works every time.

Change 2 — Add a cds config block at the bottom

Why this matters: Local cds watch is generous — it auto-bootstraps an in-memory database and skips auth without you asking. Production CAP is strict — it assumes you'll wire up real auth (XSUAA) and a real database (HANA), and refuses to fabricate defaults for either. We need to tell CAP explicitly: "for this learning task, use mocked auth and an in-memory SQLite."

The mechanic, step by step:

  1. Find the line "engines": { "node": ">=20" }.
  2. Click at the very end of that line — right after the closing curly brace }, before the line break.
  3. Type a comma , and press Enter to start a new line.
  4. Paste in this block (with the leading indentation preserved): 
      "cds": {
    "requires": {
      "auth": "mocked",
      "db": { "kind": "sqlite", "credentials": { "url": ":memory:" } }
    }
  }
  5. Save the file: Ctrl+S (Windows) or Cmd+S (Mac). If you forget to save, every command after this point will be working off the old file and you'll be confused.

BAS shows a small dot ● next to the filename in the tab if there are unsaved changes. After you save, that dot disappears. Quick visual check that you saved.

Final state — compare carefully

Your finished package.json should look exactly like this:

{
  "name": "hello-btp",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "dependencies": {
    "@sap/cds": "^9",
    "@sap/xssec": "^4",
    "@cap-js/sqlite": "^2.4"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@sap/cds-dk": "^9"
  },
  "scripts": { "start": "cds-serve" },
  "private": true,
  "engines": { "node": ">=20" },
  "cds": {
    "requires": {
      "auth": "mocked",
      "db": { "kind": "sqlite", "credentials": { "url": ":memory:" } }
    }
  }
}
Sanity-check before continuing

Look at the bottom of the BAS window. If you see a "Problems" indicator with a red number, click it — BAS lists JSON syntax issues line by line. Fix them now; the next command (npm install) will refuse to run if the file is malformed. The most common issues at this stage:

  • Missing comma between two entries
  • Extra trailing comma after the last entry of a block
  • Missing closing brace }
  • Mismatched quotes — every key and string value needs straight " quotes, not curly "smart" ones
You just cleared the biggest hurdle

If your file looks like the target above and BAS shows zero "Problems," you've done the thing most beginners get genuinely stuck on. The rest of Step 6 is running commands and watching them succeed. Genuinely well played.

Why two configs, not one

You declared both auth and db in the same cds.requires block because production CAP needs both told to it explicitly. For real apps, you'd swap auth: mocked for bound XSUAA and db: sqlite (in-memory) for bound HANA Cloud — which is exactly what Phase 2 of this course covers. The mental model carries forward unchanged; only the values change.

Install, build, log into CF, deploy

npm install
mbt build
cf login -a https://api.cf.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com
cf deploy mta_archives/hello-btp_1.0.0.mtar

What each does:

  • npm install — picks up your package.json changes, refreshes the lock file
  • mbt build — compiles your project into mta_archives/hello-btp_1.0.0.mtar. Takes 1–2 min. Success ends with INFO the MBT build of the MTA project has succeeded.
  • cf login — heads up, the terminal inside BAS is separate from the one on your laptop, so it doesn't remember your earlier login. Re-enter the same trial email and password. It's a small surprise the first time, not a mistake.
  • cf deploy — uploads the MTAR and starts the app. Takes 3–5 min. You'll see uploading → staging → starting. Don't panic at pauses.

Confirm it's live

cf apps

You should see:

name            requested state   processes   routes
hello-btp-srv   started           web:1/1     <your-route>.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com
started alone doesn't mean it works

An app can show started with broken data endpoints — that's exactly the failure mode the package.json edits prevent. Don't trust cf apps as your "done" signal. The real test is the next step.

Open your live URL — the real test

Copy your route from the cf apps output. Open in your browser with /odata/v4/catalog/Books appended:

https://<your-route>.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com/odata/v4/catalog/Books

You should see valid OData JSON. The value array can be empty (you didn't seed any data) — what matters is that the response is structured JSON with an @odata.context header, not a 500 error and not an HTML error page.

This is the moment. Your hello-btp service, running on real SAP BTP, responding to a real HTTP request. The empty value: [] is expected — you didn't seed any data. The $metadata#Books context header proves the entity exists and the deploy worked. Take the screenshot.
If /odata/v4/admin/Books says 403 Forbidden

Normal too. The admin service is scoped to require an admin role you haven't granted yourself. Always use /odata/v4/catalog/Books for validation — it's the public-readable one.

If the root URL / says "Cannot GET /"

Also normal. The pretty welcome page is a local-dev feature; it doesn't get served in production. Always validate via /odata/v4/catalog/Books, not the root URL.

You did it

You provisioned SAP BTP, scaffolded a CAP service, built a deployable archive, and pushed it live — all in one session. The URL in your browser right now is running on actual SAP cloud infrastructure. That's the same path Fortune 500 companies use to deploy their custom SAP apps. Take a screenshot of the JSON; you'll need it for the deliverable.

07Task

Save your URL.

⏱ 2 min📍 anywhere you can write

Copy your live URL somewhere safe. You'll submit it at the end along with your quiz score. The URL is the form:

https://<your-route>.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com/odata/v4/catalog/Books

Keep your cf apps output handy too — that's where the live URL was first shown to you.

Optional: stop your app to save trial resources

Once you've copied the URL, you can stop the app to save trial quota:

cf stop hello-btp-srv

Restart it any time with cf start hello-btp-srv. The URL stays the same.

Step back for a second

What you actually just did.

You provisioned a slice of real SAP cloud infrastructure (a subaccount, an org, a space). You stood up a working data service from a one-line model (CAP). You configured that service to run in production with real settings (the package.json edits). You compiled it into a deployable archive (mbt build). You pushed it through Cloud Foundry to a public URL. Then you proved the whole chain works by hitting an OData endpoint and getting back structured JSON from your service, running in SAP's cloud.

That sequence — provision → scaffold → configure → build → deploy → verify — is the spine of every SAP BTP project. The next 50 things you'll learn (HANA Cloud, XSUAA, MTA destinations, multi-tenancy, CAP custom handlers, UI5 frontends, CI/CD pipelines) all bolt onto this spine. None of them replace it. You're not starting from zero anymore.

So: the next time someone asks whether you can do BTP, you have a real answer. You've done BTP. Phase 2 of this course just adds depth to the frame you've already built.

Optional break before the quiz

The quiz is 10 questions and takes ~15 min. If your brain is fried from Step 6, take 30 min and come back. Quizzes you take immediately after intense focus tend to be worse-calibrated than ones you sit on briefly. There's no penalty for pacing yourself.

Glossary

Words in plain English.

Every technical term used in this doc, defined for someone new to SAP, cloud, or programming. Flip here whenever a word feels unfamiliar — no need to memorize anything, just look up what you need.

API
Application Programming Interface. A way for one piece of software to ask another for data or to do something. The thing you built in this task is an API.
BAS
Business Application Studio. The browser-based IDE where you do most of your work on BTP. Like VS Code, but cloud-hosted with SAP tools pre-installed.
build
The process of compiling your source code (plus dependencies) into a single deployable artifact. mbt build produces an MTAR file.
buildpack
A Cloud Foundry component that prepares your code to run. The Node.js buildpack, for example, installs dependencies and configures a Node runtime around your app.
CAP
Cloud Application Programming Model. SAP's framework for building services with very little code. Generates a working OData API from a small data model.
cds
Both a programming language (used to write CAP data models) and a command-line tool (used to scaffold, run, and configure CAP projects).
CLI
Command Line Interface. A program you control by typing commands into a terminal. btp and cf are CLIs you installed in this task.
Cloud Foundry / CF
The runtime layer inside BTP that runs your deployed code. Open-source (not SAP-invented), but SAP uses it inside BTP for application hosting.
cockpit
The web-based control panel for managing your BTP account. The visual counterpart to the btp CLI — they do the same things.
CRUD
Create, Read, Update, Delete. The four basic operations any data API performs — corresponding to HTTP verbs POST, GET, PATCH/PUT, and DELETE.
dependency
A package your code needs to run. Listed in package.json under "dependencies". Always installed, in dev and in production.
devDependency
A package only needed during development — not in production. Listed under "devDependencies". Skipped by Cloud Foundry's build step.
dev space
A pre-configured cloud-hosted development environment inside BAS. Yours runs Node, CAP tools, Git, and an editor — all without local installs.
global account
The outermost container in BTP's hierarchy. Holds one or more subaccounts. In trial, you get exactly one.
HANA Cloud
SAP's flagship cloud database. Used in real BTP apps as the production data store. You'll meet it in Phase 2 of this course.
HTTP
The protocol the web runs on. URLs use HTTP. Verbs like GET and POST are HTTP methods that say what kind of operation you're asking for.
IDE
Integrated Development Environment. A text editor with built-in extras (syntax highlighting, error checking, a terminal). BAS is one.
JSON
JavaScript Object Notation. A text format for structured data using curly braces, key-value pairs, and commas. package.json is JSON. OData responses are JSON.
JWT
JSON Web Token. A way to prove a user's identity in HTTP requests. CAP's production mode expects JWTs by default — which is why you needed auth: mocked to skip them.
LTS
Long-Term Support. A version of software (like Node.js) that gets security patches for years rather than months. You install LTS for stability.
mocked auth
A CAP setting that tells the service to pretend every request is from a generic test user, instead of checking real credentials. Fine for learning; never use in real production.
MTA
Multi-Target Application. SAP's format for packaging a deployable app with all its dependencies. cds add mta generates the manifest (mta.yaml).
MTAR
The compiled archive built from your MTA. The single file you actually run cf deploy against.
npm
Node Package Manager. The tool that downloads JavaScript libraries (like @sap/xssec) into your project. Comes bundled with Node.js.
OData
A standard for structured REST APIs. Predictable URLs, predictable query parameters, predictable JSON responses. SAP uses it everywhere.
org / space
Cloud Foundry's organizational layers. In trial, you have one org (named after your subaccount) and one space (named dev).
package.json
A file in every Node.js project that lists the project's name, version, dependencies, and configuration. The file you hand-edited in Step 6.
PATH
A list of folders your operating system searches when you type a command. Adding btp.exe's folder to PATH means you can type btp from anywhere.
PAT (Personal Access Token)
A long string GitHub gives you to act on your behalf, instead of typing a password. Treat it like a password and store it safely.
production mode
CAP's strict runtime mode used when deployed. Doesn't auto-bootstrap a database or skip auth — opposite of how cds watch behaves locally.
REST API
A style of API where you operate on resources (URLs) using HTTP verbs (GET, POST, etc.). OData is a structured flavor of REST.
route
The public URL that Cloud Foundry assigns to your deployed app. Looks like <your-name>.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com.
runtime
Software that runs your code. Node.js is your laptop runtime; Cloud Foundry is your cloud runtime.
scope
In GitHub PATs, a permission level (e.g., repo lets the token read/write repositories). In OAuth/OData, a permission claim that says what the bearer is allowed to do.
service
A piece of software that lives at a URL and responds to HTTP requests. The thing you deployed in this task is a service. "Microservice" is just a service that's small.
shell
Another word for terminal. PowerShell, bash, zsh are all shells.
SQLite
A small, file-based database. Easy to use for learning. CAP supports it natively. Real BTP apps use HANA Cloud instead.
subaccount
One workspace inside your BTP global account. Trial gets exactly one, named trial. Real organizations create one subaccount per project or per team.
terminal
A text-based way to type commands at your computer. PowerShell (Windows), Terminal (Mac), bash (Linux) — all terminals.
trial
A free, time-limited BTP account with limited resources. Cannot run real production workloads, but perfect for learning. Yours expires after a fixed period.
XSUAA
SAP's identity service. Issues JWTs and validates them. The thing you'd normally bind to your app for real auth in production. Phase 2 territory.
